title: An AI-native org isn't everyone using AI — it's assuming the org doesn't exist and rewriting it
dek: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder-type in charge of people and AI; circle leads hold the bonus-pool allocation power, and hiring requires proving AI can't do the job.
why: A 12-year hardware company's founder lays out the concrete mechanics of an org rewrite: HARO, circles, AI management trainees, how FDEs actually land — with details and the pits he fell into.
who: Founders driving AI org transformation, HR leaders and business owners — especially at hardware or consumer electronics companies who want to move the org but don't know where to start.
skip: After 1:04:25 the chit-chat and outro music can be skipped.

points.h: AI-native starts by assuming the org doesn't exist
points.body: Chen Bin's definition of an AI-native organization is not ‘everyone should use AI well’ but starting from AI and asking again: can AI do this thing, and as far as possible don't let a person do it. The harsher step is to assume the original organization and processes don't exist — ‘they shouldn't even exist’ — and go back to the state of a one-person startup to redesign roles and processes. So this is not accelerating existing processes, it's tearing the processes down first and rebuilding. He admits this is mainly aimed at the core org builders, not a slogan shouted at everyone.

points.h: HARO's lead comes from tech, not HR
points.body: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO (Human AI Resource Office), but Chen Bin stresses it is not an ordinary HR+IT: the lead must understand the business, and he picked the old partner who co-founded with him and has done technology, product, CEO, R&D, brand and IT. The logic is inverted — the old HR lead leaned toward people and was insensitive to AI; now a tech-oriented person leads, and he is given an HR BP who is sensitive to people. Under this department sits a solid-line AIO (the former IT team, which will build agents in future) and a dotted-line FDE.

points.h: Agent Builder and FDE are two kinds of people for now
points.body: Chen Bin draws the line clearly: an Agent Builder leans technical and can build an agent; an FDE has to go into the business front line, map supply, planning and procurement processes, and is best a business expert. Long term one person might cover it; short term it must be two kinds of people working together. They did not copy Anker's approach of pulling people out of work and locking them away for a month, because they don't have that much slack; instead people from the business spend 30% to 50% of their energy doing AI-ification alongside their day jobs. The company also set AI proficiency levels L1 to L4, with L2 and above called ‘AI navigators’ and above that ‘pilots’.

points.h: Circles erase functional power; circle leads hold the bonus pool
points.body: Lockin's circles differ from project teams and Huawei's matrix: the matrix is product line plus function on two axes, while a circle is a small team with an end-to-end value loop, deliberately erasing functional power and boundaries so the circle lead's power grows. The company gives the circle a bonus pool, and the circle lead decides how to split it — even how much to give himself — while HR and functional departments only have an advisory voice. Chen Bin says at this stage the ‘fighting’ line dominates; the functional line may in future become something like a technology committee, but within six months to a year of the transformation the front line calls the shots first.

points.h: Experience can turn into a burden
points.body: Chen Bin says AI management trainees naturally started using AI from university in 2023, have no fear of doing things, and use it more than the veterans. His exact words: ‘sometimes experience instead becomes a burden’, and the worst is the half-through-water type — experience hasn't arrived but they feel very experienced and can't change. Veterans have framework thinking and systematic thinking as a foundation, but which processes and which roles can be removed is easier for the clear-headed to judge. The bar for AI management trainees is internal AI level L2 or above, requiring skill use and agent building; only L3 can author workflows.

points.h: R&D turns fast, marketing turns slow
points.body: Chen Bin admits transformation speed varies a lot by department: technical R&D tied to software and coding is easiest, because writing code every day gives positive feedback; marketing and brand are slow, because after publishing more content they ask ‘so what’ — did it bring revenue growth and higher bonuses. He also mentions a real conflict: people doing design and content feel AI can only accelerate volume, not raise quality, and 60-point output doesn't stick. His response is to give everyone an operating mindset: whether content drives conversion is the standard.

points.h: Three rounds of sign-ups: stand up again, sit down again
points.body: Lockin ran three rounds of internal sign-ups: the first for incremental roles, such as a dozen or two company-level agents and the corresponding Agent Builders and FDEs; the second for roles missing after circles formed, such as a content marketing Agent Builder; the third to keep filling gaps. Applicants first do a self-assessment to find what they're good at, then give a three-to-five-minute defense, and after the judges score, AI is used to analyze the meeting notes and the talk for matching. Of a hundred applicants, twenty or thirty may be chosen. Chen Bin says both the mechanism and the results were very good.

points.h: To hire, you must first prove AI can't do it
points.body: After a circle picks off people from an original department, if the boss wants to backfill, logically there are only two channels: find an AI management trainee, or use more AI tokens. If you really must rehire, it goes to Chen Bin for special approval, and you have to explain why a management trainee won't do and why AI won't do. Chen Bin says ‘logically he has no channel left’. They plan to hire 50 AI management trainees by year-end and are already close to 20. Xiaofei's role at Lockin is like a strategic HR, a CHO as a service, doing the AI-native transformation together with Chen Bin.

Chen Bin says inside the company he is actually the most radical one, often held back by everyone urging caution. On Huawei IPD and similar accumulated practice, his judgment is: AI can only rework processes that were already unreasonable and especially redundant; IPD itself is very reasonable and can only be accelerated. For example, SP to BP, from strategy to execution, used to take three months to half a year, now two months — a doubling of efficiency — but the nodes like five looks and three settings remain, just three weeks becoming three days. Training a product line manager used to take 10 to 15 years, now three to five, but the rotation posts that should be rotated cannot be skipped.

points.h: Not everyone should run this fast
points.body: Chen Bin's advice to three kinds of bosses — milk tea shops, PCB factories, call centers — is to look at the real value AI brings in that industry: the more traditional the industry, the lower the value, and you can wait until platforms like Doubao and Volcano Engine mature before choosing, with lower trial-and-error cost. But the more frontier the tech company, the earlier it should embrace AI, because technology changes a lot and the market changes fast, and decision quality matters more. He specifically notes that before physical AI takes off, PCB factories and the like should be cautious and not move first; milk tea shops are more channel- and operations-driven, and AI can quickly build a feedback loop from the user end to the supply chain end, so its effect is bigger.

quotes.text: I think a native organization probably starts from AI first — whatever AI can do, try not to have a person do it. Think AI-native first, think about this thing, and even this process, which logically should be restructured.

It used to be functional, right? Now I'm an end-to-end small team with a value loop, and I even deliberately erase the functional power, or the boundaries, or take them away — make functional power smaller, make the circle's power, or the circle lead's power, bigger.

Actually sometimes experience instead becomes a burden. It's better to have it — it's often the half-through-water type that's scary: their experience hasn't arrived, but they feel they're already very experienced, right? Can't change.

As far as possible we fill with AI, right? Prioritize using AI — whatever AI can fill, let AI fill it. Unless it can't be filled. If it can't be filled, then internally we say: either you say find an AI management trainee to fill it, or use more AI tokens.

It used to take at least three months to half a year; now we do SP to BP in two months, right? At least a doubling of efficiency. But the process itself hasn't changed — it's just that where I used to hold five meetings, it becomes three meetings, two meetings.

Actually look at the real value AI brings in this industry. I think the more traditional the industry, the lower the value it brings, indeed a bit lower. Lower means you can, as it were, wait until these — like us, the ones who fall in the pit and play around, right? Or like Doubao at work, Volcano Engine, the ones doing better — and then choose. That's fine.
